source.title: Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026/27 — Corporate Governance and Audit Committee, 30 January 2026

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026/27 — Corporate Governance and Audit Committee, 30 January 2026

facts.note: Table 1 and Table 2 (p.5) foot exactly. Loans CFR less external borrowing equals internal borrowing in every year. §2.11 puts the three-year gross borrowing requirement at up to £525.6m.

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy and Investment Strategy 2026/27 — Corporate Governance and Audit Committee, 30 January 2026

summary.text:
Read on the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Corporate Governance and Audit on 30 January 2026, alongside the mid-year monitoring report to the same committee on 28 November 2025 for the loan-book detail. Table 1 and Table 2 in the strategy foot exactly in every one of the four forecast years, and the balance sheet identity closes to the pound: CFR £1,001.5m less PFI £79.1m less other deferred £0.3m is the £922.1m Loans CFR, less external borrowing £781.9m is the £140.2m of internal borrowing.

The hook is a dated, testable assumption. §2.6 carries Arlingclose's central view that Bank Rate will fall through 2026 to around 3.25%. §2.19 then makes that view load-bearing: 'it is therefore likely to be more cost effective over the medium-term to either use internal resources, or to borrow short-term loans instead, which can then be re-financed when rates are lower.' Bank Rate is 3.75% today and the December cut was 5-4 against holding at 4.00%. Behind that assumption sits §2.11's £525.6m gross borrowing requirement over the three years to 31.03.29, with the drivers unusually named — Our Cultural Heart, town/district centre regeneration, two Safety Valve special schools and Housing.

The mid-year report confirms the position: total borrowing £789.7m at 30.09.25 at a weighted 4.35%. Two smaller items of interest: £7.0m of Loan Stock is still outstanding at 11.60%, the highest non-PWLB legacy coupon in our library, and £30.0m of LOBOs run with call windows across 25/26 and 26/27, where the strategy states the Council will accept a call and repay — matching the pattern we have seen at Harrow, Staffordshire and Wolverhampton this year.

The loan-book reconciliation did not tie. Our bc-loans file at 30/09/25 returns no outstanding loans because the file's start dates for Kirklees loans sit later than that date; the whole file holds 85 loans totalling £680.4m against the paper's £616.9m of PWLB. Per PIPELINE.md the loan-book claim is left out of the email. The paper is nonetheless a full read — balance sheet, borrowing strategy, MRP, investments and prudential indicators are all here — and there is a strong hook without it. Officer addresses are not published; front sheet gives phone only.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 treasury strategy that went to Corporate Governance and Audit on 30 January and Council on 25 February, currently in force, ahead of what will be the mid-year monitoring report to the same committee in November. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is clearly laid out and the balance sheet foots to the pound, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique. We read the 25/26 mid-year report alongside it for the loan-book detail.

The reason we wrote is a single sentence in section 2.19. Because short-term rates are expected to fall further, the strategy says it will be 'more cost effective over the medium-term to either use internal resources, or to borrow short-term loans instead, which can then be re-financed when rates are lower.' That sits directly on Arlingclose's central view at 2.6, that Bank Rate will fall through 2026 to around 3.25%. Bank Rate is 3.75% today; the December cut was 5-4 with the minority favouring holding at 4.00%; and the one-year SONIA is trading around 4.11%, the two-year around 4.21%. That's not a criticism of the forecast — every adviser has moved this year — but it is a live divergence and it's the assumption your medium-term plan is priced against. We publish the market-implied path rather than a house view, deliberately, because it updates every day.

That matters here more than in most councils because of what's queued behind it. Section 2.11 puts the three-year gross borrowing requirement at up to £525.6m to fund the Loans CFR rise from £922.1m to £1,208.8m, one of the larger three-year programmes we've read this year, and the 2026/27 authorised limit is £1,047.0m. If the central case plays out you save real money by staying short. If it doesn't, several hundred million rolls at rates closer to today's than to 3.25%. Your Appendix D interest rate risk indicator — a £5.2m one-year revenue impact of a 1% rise — accommodates that intent almost exactly: at 1% it implies around £520m of borrowing that could reprice in a year.

For the market you'd be drawing into, July's sector PWLB activity was thin at about £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%. The month-by-month breakdown, split by HRA and General Fund and by council, is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. What it also shows is how the inter-authority market has picked up the strain when PWLB months go quiet — you drew £67.5m from other authorities in Q1–Q3 at 4.10% to 4.90%, inside a library range this year that ran from 4.15% (Gloucestershire) to 8.50% (Cornwall for four days). No single council sees that distribution from its own trades.

Two smaller things. The £7.0m of Loan Stock at 11.60% in your mid-year Table 2 is the highest non-PWLB legacy coupon we've read on any council — about £812k a year of interest on a £7m position. And the £30.0m of LOBOs with call windows across 2025/26 and 2026/27: 2.22 says you'll take the option to repay if called, which matches a pattern we've read repeatedly this year at Harrow, Staffordshire, Wolverhampton and Kent, where every call has been refused. We track those windows and outcomes across the sector because no single council can see them from its own file.

One caveat on our data — our PWLB file for Kirklees doesn't reconcile cleanly to your 30 September position at 4.27%, so this note doesn't quote our loan-book totals back at you. What we do publish daily is a per-loan valuation of your book against the DMO's premature repayment curve, at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Nothing follows from it: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real settlement. The point is only that with £525m of drawing ahead, the spread between new borrowing and premature repayment moves in ways worth watching.

On training, four fit Kirklees. SONIA Forward Curve & OIS and Reading the PWLBpredict speak to 2.6 and 2.19. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes to your £67.5m of LA borrowing so far this year. The Capital Strategy is written for members and is the right frame for a £525m three-year figure. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: 26/27 Treasury Management Strategy Report (30 January 2026); Half Yearly Monitoring report on Treasury Management activities 2025/26 (28 November 2025).
